title: Embouchure and teeth position on the mouthpiece
summary: Russell asks about embouchure; Tio says Lorenzo pressed on his upper teeth without biting, and his father and uncle taught pupils not to bite, keeping the tongue free.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well, I was going to ask about the position of the teeth on the mouthpiece. Most clarinetists that I know put their upper teeth, they put the lower lip on top of the lower teeth, even then they bite on them.
But a few people used their lip over both teeth. Well, then I... Marty Bigard does that. I wonder if he learned that from your brother. Do you know how your brother did or your father and the...

No, my brother had a way of his upper teeth. He would bite onto the mouthpiece? Upper teeth. Well, he had pressure against his upper teeth. In other words, he played clarinet so long that his teeth had been ground down in the shape of a mouthpiece. Mm-hmm. But for his biting on the lower teeth, no he didn't. He never, never... He covered those.
He had... In better words, that's the reason why he could use his tongue so well. Mm-hmm. On the...
Did your father and uncle too, if you remember, did they bite onto the... No, they had...
Get their teeth onto the... No, they had... When they taught a scholar, they tried not to make him bite it. Because when you're biting an instrument, you're... You're fouling it.
I think what Bill means, he means that they teach him to rest their teeth on the... Yeah, I know what you mean.

Yeah. But oftentimes, uh... Sometime you can foul it that way, you understand? The best thing is to keep the lower teeth from it. Yeah, the lower teeth. I'm wondering about the upper teeth, though, too. And let the instrument rest in on your lips. Yes.

Because you've got a better pressure, you've got a better way of using your tongue. I was just wondering about the upper teeth, though. If they covered the upper teeth, too. Some people, I think they call that the French system, a double embouchure, putting the lip over the upper teeth, too. And the upper teeth, too. Some people do that. Do you know if they ever taught that? Or played that way?

I'll tell you what. Here's the position that he would use his clarinet. If he had his clarinet, well, uh... When he'd stick it in his mouth, he would always, mostly have the pressure up above on his upper teeth. Yeah. He would never have his pressure down on you. He always had his upper teeth. In better words, if he turned and looked at you like that, he turned... But the clarinet would never go down. He kept the pressure on his upper teeth, not on his lower teeth. But the lip, of course, would close in. Yeah, sure. I don't know how close his teeth was to the reed, but I know that he never would bite it. Like you said, biting it. Yeah, I don't know. That would be biting. That would be closing your teeth on it. Because I don't believe... A fellow biting a reed... He's then putting strain on yourself because... Yes. ...for the pressure... He's putting it, he's pumping from here. Where you could say... Do-do-do-do-do-do-do... With your teeth. With your tongue. Where if you had your teeth in your mouth, then you'd be... You'd have to do... Hoo! Yeah. You'd have to pump it from here. Yeah, that's right, yeah. You see? And that, you had to blow it from your lungs. Where if you had your teeth free, well you could toot it from your tongue.
